commons:25371411.summary: Christ sits frontally on a cushioned throne before a crenellated wall, blessing with his right hand and holding a jewelled book in his left, his head framed by a gold cross-nimbus and flanked by the letters IHS XPS. Plants spring up around the throne and the whole is enclosed in a frame of interlace and ornament. Painted for Charlemagne, this serene image stands at the very beginning of the Carolingian revival of book painting.
facts: The manuscript was commissioned by Charlemagne and his queen Hildegard on 7 October 781 and completed on 30 April 783; its dedication poem names the scribe Godescalc.
It is the earliest known manuscript from Charlemagne's Court School and is written in gold and silver ink on purple-dyed parchment.
Its six full-page miniatures are the four Evangelists, this Christ in Majesty and the Fountain of Life.
commons:25371411.notes: The Court School's location is often given as Aachen; the folio number was not verified. Held by the Bibliothèque nationale de France, Paris.
commons:25371411.original_title: Évangéliaire dit de Charlemagne ou de Godescalc : Jésus-Christ

commons:83842993.summary: A small, almost transparent veil, about 17.5 by 24 cm, bearing the face of a man with open eyes, a long nose and a light beard, shown here in its silver reliquary frame in the Capuchin sanctuary at Manoppello. Local tradition holds that an unknown pilgrim brought it to the town in 1508; some modern writers have identified it with the Veil of Veronica once shown in Rome, but there is no documentary evidence connecting the cloth with Rome or with the Passion. Most researchers regard the face as an artificially made image whose style resembles works of the late Middle Ages or early Renaissance, while it remains for many pilgrims a moving image of the Holy Face.
facts: Its history — the arrival of the veil in 1508, its passing through the Leonelli and De Fabritiis families and its gift to the Capuchins — is known from the Relatione historica of Fr Donato da Bomba, based on research begun in 1640.
No samples have been allowed for laboratory analysis; a recent study concluded that linen is the most probable material, although the claim that it is woven of sea silk (byssus) is often repeated.
Pope Benedict XVI visited the sanctuary on 1 September 2006.
commons:83842993.notes: Dating is uncertain: no technical dating exists. y=1500 reflects the stylistic judgement (late medieval / early Renaissance) and the traditional arrival in 1508. Claims of a first-century origin (H. Pfeiffer, P. Badde) are unsupported by evidence.

cur:catacombs2-domitilla-arcosolium-magi.summary: The wall around this arched tomb niche is painted with a small cycle of salvation. Above the arch the three Magi bring their gifts to the Virgin seated with the Child, while to the left Christ, holding his rod, raises Lazarus; the slide label also names Moses striking the rock and the healing of the paralytic, who appears below at the left carrying his bed. Christ's birth, his miracles and the water from the rock together speak of the life promised to the one buried here.
facts: The slide label reads 'Vierge et 3 mages, Lazare, Moïse et rocher, paralytique (IV s.)', and the Leuven record cites Wilpert, Die Malereien der Katakomben Roms, plate 238.
The Catacomb of Domitilla on the Via Ardeatina is one of the largest in Rome, and contains several distinct paintings of the Magi.
cur:catacombs2-domitilla-arcosolium-magi.notes: Known only from this tinted glass-slide reproduction of Wilpert's plate; the placement of each scene is described from the image and may be imprecise.

cur:manuscripts-trier-apocalypse-ephesus.summary: A bust of Christ with a cross-staff looks out from a band of blue sky at the upper left, while John stands at the right holding a scroll beside a garden of flowering trees — the 'tree of life, which is in the midst of the paradise of God' promised to those who overcome. Below, rivers and waters flow across the page.
facts: The Trier Apocalypse contains 74 full-page drawings illustrating about 150 episodes of the Book of Revelation; it is one of the earliest illustrated Apocalypse manuscripts to survive.
Its pictures are thought to copy a late antique model of the 4th–6th century, which explains features such as books shown as scrolls and Christ as the beardless Logos.

cur:manuscripts-egberti-pool-of-bethesda.summary: Christ stands among his apostles and stretches out his hand toward the sick man lying on a green bed, while above, an angel descends to stir the water of the pool where another man bathes.
facts: Egbert gave the book to the church of St Paulin in Trier, where it was used in services until the 18th century; it has been in the Trier city library since 1810 and was added to UNESCO's Memory of the World register in 2004 with other Reichenau manuscripts.
Seven of its miniatures are attributed to the anonymous 'Master of the Registrum Gregorii', who worked in Trier.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-70-christ.summary: The bearded psalmist, holding a lute and pointing to his mouth, stands before a tabernacle and asks help from the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos, who holds a book in both hands — 'O God, thou hast taught me from my youth' — with two angels. Beside him lie a harp and what looks like a pipe organ, and demons below threaten him. The psalm of old age is pictured as a lifelong conversation with the divine teacher.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
It reached Canterbury by about 1000, where it was copied three times in the Middle Ages: the Harley Psalter, the Eadwine Psalter and the Anglo-Catalan Psalter.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-70-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-141-chris.summary: Kneeling in the open doorway of a prison, the psalmist lifts his hand to the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos, who stands on a hill with three angels and four of the righteous — 'bring my soul out of prison' — while an angel with a cross-staff points out his plight. From Christ's hill flow the four rivers of Paradise, from which small naked figures drink, 'my portion in the land of the living'. It is the upper drawing of folio 79v.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
The psalter was made in or near Reims, probably under Archbishop Ebbo (816–835); some scholars argue for a date around 850 under his successor Hincmar.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-141-chris.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server. This folio carries two drawings; the crop shows the one for this text.

cur:manuscripts2-escorial-son-of-man-on-.summary: At the top of a brilliant yellow page sits one 'like unto the Son of man' on a white cloud, his head encircled by a red halo, while angels fly about him; below, angels reap the harvest with sickles, gather the grapes and tread the winepress of the wrath of God. The Son of Man on the cloud is Christ coming in judgement.
facts: The Escorial Beatus has 151 surviving leaves and 52 miniatures; it was probably made at San Millán de la Cogolla and was already in the Escorial library in the 16th century.
Its figures, with huge eyes and boldly patterned drapery, are among the most expressive in the Beatus tradition.
cur:manuscripts2-escorial-son-of-man-on-.notes: Folio number not given on Commons; the file name '120' may refer to the folio.

cur:manuscripts2-menologion-nativity.summary: In a rocky landscape on a gold ground, the Virgin reclines beside the manger in a cave where the Christ child lies, with the ox and ass looking on; angels bend down from above, a shepherd approaches, Joseph sits in thought at the lower left, and midwives bathe the newborn in a basin. The composition gathers the whole Byzantine Christmas iconography into a single, finely painted miniature.
facts: The Menologion of Basil II, made at Constantinople for Emperor Basil II (976–1025), holds about 430 miniatures by eight painters whose names — among them Pantoleon, Michael of Blachernai and Nestor — are written beside each image.
It covers only the first half of the church year, September to February, and passed through the hands of Ludovico Sforza, Duke of Milan, before Pope Paul V received it for the Vatican Library.

cur:monumental-santa-costanza-traditio-l.summary: Christ, in golden robes and with a halo, stands on the mount of Paradise from which the four rivers flow, raising his right hand and handing a scroll to Peter, while Paul acclaims him from the other side; sheep and palm trees complete the scene. The scroll bears the words DOMINUS PACEM DAT, 'the Lord gives peace'. This 'giving of the law' was one of the defining images of Christ in Early Christian Rome.
facts: Wikipedia describes the two apse mosaics of Santa Costanza as perhaps the earliest surviving images of Christ as ruler of the world; their date (variously 4th, 5th or 7th century) remains debated, and both have suffered from restoration.
The scroll's inscription DOMINUS PACEM DAT ('the Lord gives peace') replaces the more usual DOMINUS LEGEM DAT ('the Lord gives the law').
The building was erected as an imperial mausoleum, traditionally for Constantina, daughter of Constantine I, who died in 354.

cur:objects2-walters-enamel-pectoral-cro.summary: A small hollow cross of sheet gold, its rounded arms each marked by three bosses and a pierced cross, holds at its centre a roped medallion of cloisonné enamel: on one side a standing figure of Christ, on the other a bust of Christ, worked in blue, red and green. Worn on the breast, it joined the sign of the cross with the face of the Saviour.
facts: The museum notes that the surfaces are slightly crushed and the lower arm bent, signs of the cross's long use.
It was bought by Henry Walters from the Paris dealer Léon Gruel in 1928.

feat:hofmann-christ-and-the-rich-young-r.summary: Christ turns toward a richly dressed young man and gestures to the poor man crouching in the shadows, inviting him to sell all he has and follow. The young man, richly dressed in silks, hesitates and draws back slightly. Hofmann's gentle, dignified Christ became one of the most widely reproduced images of Jesus in the Protestant world.
facts: It was bought by John D. Rockefeller Jr. and, together with Hofmann's Christ in Gethsemane and Christ in the Temple, now hangs at Riverside Church in New York.
Reproductions of Hofmann's Christ became especially beloved in American Protestant and Latter-day Saint homes and churches.
The contrast of shimmering silk and the beggar's rags makes visible the choice the young man faces.
